seoDescription: Bring Her Back (2025) horror movie review. Sally Hawkins' unhinged grief, Danny and Michael Philippou's bleak occult rituals, and a devastating gut-punch ending.
title: Bring Her Back
excerpt: A bleak, tragic, and genuinely surprising horror film from the Philippou brothers with Sally Hawkins delivering unhinged grief and a gut-wrenching ending.
body: The Philippou brothers proved with Talk to Me that they know how to twist grief into pure dread, and Bring Her Back doubles down on that in the best way possible. It starts off looking like your standard creepy foster home setup, but it takes sharp, mean left turns that genuinely caught me off guard.

The story kicks off with Andy and his stepsister Piper losing their dad. With nowhere else to go, they get placed with Laura, played by Sally Hawkins (who you definitely remember from The Shape of Water). On paper she seems like the sweet, nurturing foster mom you pray for after a tragedy, but Hawkins plays her with this razor-thin edge where you immediately sense something is completely broken underneath. She lost her own daughter in an accident, and she is dead set on doing whatever sick occult ritual it takes to bring her back.

Then you meet Oliver. The trailers make him look like a creepy mute kid, but the reality is way worse. He is being used as a literal vessel. Laura has got him trapped behind this white line on the floor, and as long as he stays inside it, he is locked in this horrific trance. The feeding rituals she forces on him are straight-up repulsive. She is following instructions off old VHS tapes, force-feeding him to bulk him up so he can puke it back out to manifest her dead daughter. It gets even creepier when you realize Oliver can project hallucinations using DNA. Laura plucking hair off their dead dad at the funeral just to feed it to Oliver so Andy sees his ghost in the shower was a brilliant, unsettling touch.

Piper, the stepsister, is the absolute heart of this movie. She is legally blind, seeing mostly silhouettes. I actually looked it up after watching because her performance felt so grounded, and sure enough, the actress Sora Wong actually has low vision in real life. That makes her performance phenomenal. When horror movies have visually impaired characters, it usually feels like cheap gimmickry or pure helplessness. Here, every time she is moving through that house or feeling her way around, the tension is suffocating.

There is a moment halfway through where Oliver is practically shoving a knife down his own throat. Andy tackles him across that white threshold, and the second Oliver crosses the line, the trance breaks and he whispers, "Help me." That gave me chills. Laura losing her mind over that boundary break shows you just how calculated and desperate she really is.

The third act goes for the jugular. Andy brings a caseworker back to the house to blow the lid off the place, and things spiral into chaos. Most modern horror films would let Andy be the hero who gets everyone out. Not this one. Andy gets tackled into a puddle, and Laura literally drowns him with her bare hands. That death hit like a ton of bricks. He was only a month or two away from turning eighteen, just about to age out of the system and get him and Piper a normal life. Having him die right there was a bold, genuinely devastating twist that I did not see coming.

Piper's escape attempt in the dark is pure anxiety. She is bumping into walls and furniture trying to get out, and Laura catches her and tries to drown her too. But when Piper gasps out "Mom," Laura hesitates just long enough out of pure grief for Piper to scratch her, break free, and sprint into the street where a car picks her up. Meanwhile, Oliver is staggering after her, hacking up blood, until he spots his own missing child poster. That spark of memory kicks in, and he hurls his own body over the salt line to snap out of it.

Seeing the police find Oliver at the end, battered, bleeding, with his teeth completely wrecked, whispering "Please help me, my name is Oliver," was such a relief. Laura is left floating dead in the water alongside the dead daughter she kept in the freezer. It is a bleak, tragic, incredibly well-crafted horror film that commits to its premise without pulling its punches.
verdict: 8/10: A bleak, tragic, and genuinely surprising horror film from the Philippou brothers with Sally Hawkins delivering unhinged grief and a gut-wrenching ending.
